Reading the lead-mining landscape

An extract from our Pennine industrial history series.

Hushes come first

A hush is a scar left by releasing dammed water down a hillside to strip the soil and expose the vein. On the Grassington moors most hushes date from the 1690s to the 1750s.

Then levels and shafts

Once the vein was found, horizontal levels were driven in from the valley side. A level of 500 metres could take a decade to cut by hand.

Dressing floors last

Ore was crushed, washed and sorted on dressing floors near the level mouth. Their flat platforms and buddle pits are usually the clearest surviving earthworks.
